Explain a GRIMMER test step by step

Source: R/grimmer-explain.R
grimmer_explain.Rd

grimmer_explain() tests a single mean and SD like grimmer() does, but also lays out the calculation in plain words. It starts with the GRIM test of the mean, as in grim_explain(), and goes on to the sum of squares that each possible sum implies with the SD.

The text is built from the numbers that decide the test itself, so it always agrees with grimmer().

Usage

grimmer_explain(
  x,
  sd,
  n,
  digits_x,
  digits_sd,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  sd_meaning = c("sd_sample", "sd_pop", "sd_sample_or_pop", "se"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  symmetric = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

Numeric. The reported mean.

sd

Numeric. The reported standard deviation.

n

Integer. The reported sample size.

digits_x

Integer. The number of decimal places in x, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

digits_sd

Integer. The number of decimal places in sd, including trailing zeros. There is no default, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4).

items_averaged

Integer. As in grim(), for x and sd.

data_type

String. As in grim(): "integer" or "continuous". No default. Continuous data can have any mean and any SD of 0 or more, but a single value only an SD of 0.

sd_meaning

String. What sd really is. "sd_sample" (the default) is the sample SD, which divides by n - 1; "sd_pop" is the population SD, which divides by n; "sd_sample_or_pop" accepts either; "se" is the standard error of the mean, the sample SD divided by sqrt(n), reported as if it were an SD. See Defaults and SD meaning in grimmer().

rounding

String. The rounding method assumed to have produced x. Default is "up_or_down", which accepts either direction; see Defaults in grim(). The others are "up_from_or_down_from", "ceiling_or_floor", "up", "down", "even", "up_from", "down_from", "ceiling", "floor", "trunc", "anti_trunc", "ties_up", "ties_down", "ties_away", "ties_zero", and "ties_even". See vignette("rounding-options", package = "roundwork").

threshold

Numeric. For rounding = "up_from", "down_from", or "up_from_or_down_from", the point within a step at which rounding switches direction, in tenths of a step. Default is 5. Ignored otherwise.

symmetric

Logical. If TRUE, negative numbers are rounded like their absolute values (-2.5 like 2.5) under "up", "down", and the "*_from" methods. Default is FALSE. Must not be TRUE with a "ties_*" rounding method, which already fixes the direction; see roundwork::reround().

Value

An object of class scrutiny_explain: a list with the result as consistency (TRUE, FALSE, or NA), the explanation's paragraphs, and the test and its inputs. It prints as the explanation.

Examples

grimmer_explain(
  x = 5.23,
  sd = 2.55,
  n = 35,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> GRIMMER test: x = 5.23, sd = 2.55, n = 35, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"
#> 
#> The mean was reported as 5.23, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming
#> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from
#> 5.225 to 5.235.
#> 
#> The mean of 35 integers is their sum divided by 35. So the sum must be from
#> 5.225 * 35 = 182.875 to 5.235 * 35 = 183.225.
#> 
#> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 183 is in this range:
#> 183 / 35 = 5.2286, which rounds to 5.23.
#> 
#> The SD was reported as 2.55, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could
#> have been anything from 2.545 to 2.555.
#> 
#> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you
#> get by squaring each of the 35 values and adding them up. It is
#> (35 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 35. The values are integers, so their squares are
#> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its
#> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if
#> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even.
#> 
#> With a sum of 183, the sum of squares is from
#> 34 * 2.545^2 + 183^2 / 35 = 1177.0474 to 34 * 2.555^2 + 183^2 / 35 = 1178.7814.
#> The only integer in this range is 1178, which is even, but 183 is odd.
#> 
#> ==> Inconsistent

grimmer_explain(
  x = 5.23,
  sd = 2.55,
  n = 31,
  digits_x = 2,
  digits_sd = 2,
  items_averaged = 1,
  data_type = "integer"
)
#> GRIMMER test: x = 5.23, sd = 2.55, n = 31, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"
#> 
#> The mean was reported as 5.23, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming
#> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from
#> 5.225 to 5.235.
#> 
#> The mean of 31 integers is their sum divided by 31. So the sum must be from
#> 5.225 * 31 = 161.975 to 5.235 * 31 = 162.285.
#> 
#> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 162 is in this range:
#> 162 / 31 = 5.2258, which rounds to 5.23.
#> 
#> The SD was reported as 2.55, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could
#> have been anything from 2.545 to 2.555.
#> 
#> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you
#> get by squaring each of the 31 values and adding them up. It is
#> (31 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 31. The values are integers, so their squares are
#> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its
#> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if
#> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even.
#> 
#> With a sum of 162, the sum of squares is from
#> 30 * 2.545^2 + 162^2 / 31 = 1040.8914 to 30 * 2.555^2 + 162^2 / 31 = 1042.4214.
#> The integers from 1041 to 1042 are in this range, so one of them is even, like
#> 162.
#> 
#> ==> Consistent
